tier_reason: README Performance tables compare smmalloc against the CRT malloc baseline (the 'crt' row; smmalloc_perf01.cpp defines it as malloc/free) on a named CPU (i7-2600) and on PS4. The benchmark code is public, but no compiler or flags are stated, so these are first-party numbers with partial methodology: Tier C.

corrections.baseline: CRT malloc/free (C runtime heap, the allocator under default operator new)
corrections.claimed_speedup: ~40 cycles/op with thread cache (README feature claim); ~3.9x CRT at 1 thread (92,615,384 vs 23,853,865) and ~2.6x CRT at 5 threads (38,303,161 vs 14,636,381) on i7-2600 (derived from page data); ~8.1x CRT at 1 thread on PS4 (36,065,574 vs 4,444,444) (derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Multi-threaded small-object malloc/free stress test (the current harness uses random 16-80 byte sizes). The README tables give unlabeled per-allocator counts; the current harness, smmalloc_perf01.cpp with smmalloc_test_impl.inl, computes ops/sec. Covers 1-5 threads on Windows 10/i7-2600 and 1-4 threads on PS4, comparing smmalloc against CRT malloc, rpmalloc, Hoard, ltalloc, dlmalloc(+mutex) and mspace (PS4 only).

notes: All table numbers check out. The ratios were missing the '(derived from page data)' marker, so it is now added. The CRT baseline is malloc/free, not operator new, and the README does not label the units (the harness computes ops/sec). Metadata matches: MIT, 335 stars, last commit 2023-10-13, stale.

tier_reason: The dashboard's embedded data for the Genoa platform shows dispenso vs tbb in summing_for. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/summing_for_benchmark.cpp), and the page states the compiler (GNU 11.5.0, C++20), the build (CMake Release) and the CPU (AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 166 cores). One weakness: the CPU is only a VM model string with no SKU.

corrections.caveats: The claimed points are favorable picks from mixed results against TBB. On the same Genoa data TBB is faster at 1M elements with 128 threads (47.6us vs 47.8us) and 166 threads (44.2us vs 49.3us). It is also faster at 100M elements with 1-4 and 32 threads (e.g. 2 threads: 14.55ms vs 16.72ms; 32 threads: 2.47ms vs 2.69ms). OpenMP beats dispenso at many points. The 'Future/Async Tree Build' chart, the advertised std::async comparison, has zero data points on all four platforms. The dashboard does, however, hold direct std comparisons with real data: dispenso::RWLock vs std::shared_mutex (serial, 2 iterations: 6.07ms vs 11.52ms), OnceFunction vs std::function (small move: 20.8ns vs 148.4ns), and ConcurrentVector vs std::vector/std::deque. Flags are the CMake Release defaults (cxx_flags lists only -I/tmp/folly-shim), and the CPU is the VM string 'AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor' with no SKU. The 1K-element runs show >50x gaps dominated by TBB dispatch overhead and were excluded.

notes: All three claimed TBB data points match the embedded PLATFORMS JSON exactly. The page also has std::shared_mutex, std::function and std::vector comparisons (libstdc++ on Linux/GCC 11.5, MSVC STL on Windows, libc++ on macOS). The orchestrator may want separate stdlib-baseline records for those. The default-branch last commit is 2026-09-02 (pushed_at is 2026-09-03).

tier_reason: The runtime-benchmarks README summary table has TooManyCooks and tbb columns with the exact numbers claimed. The benchmark code is public (cpp/TooManyCooks/*.cpp vs cpp/tbb/*.cpp, driven by build_and_bench_all.py). Compiler (Clang 21.1.7), flags (-O3 -march=native) and CPU (EPYC 7742) are all stated.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark suite (tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks, 36 stars) is maintained by the TooManyCooks author, so it is not a fully independent third party, though its code, compiler, flags and CPU model are public and reproducible. GitHub reports the suite's license as NOASSERTION, but its LICENSE file is the Unlicense. TMC does not top this shootout: citor (1.06x) and libfork (1.18x) have better mean-ratio-to-best than TMC (1.32x). The baseline beaten is oneTBB, not std::async/std::thread/std::future. No head-to-head benchmark against raw std::async/std::thread was found for this project.

notes: All four ratios and the mean-ratio figures match the TooManyCooks row and the tbb row. Metadata matches: BSL-1.0, 281 stars, last commit 2026-09-22, active. The only fix is the runtime-benchmarks license in caveats: the LICENSE file is the Unlicense, not an unidentified license.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C to A. The paper's methodology (Sec. V-A) names 2x Xeon Platinum 8480+ (112 cores), Clang 18.0.0 at the highest optimization setting with asserts disabled, and pinned library versions. The artifact code is in libfork bench/source/{fib,integrate,matmul,nqueens,uts}/{libfork,tbb,omp,taskflow}.cpp. The independent tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks suite (Clang 21.1.7 -O3 -march=native, EPYC 7742) corroborates it with explicit flags: libfork 36,519us vs tbb 142,887us on skynet.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper conclusion: up to 7.5x faster and 19x less memory than oneTBB, up to 24x faster and 24x less memory than OpenMP (libomp), and up to 100x faster and several orders of magnitude less memory than taskflow. The 7.5x/24x peaks are for fib at 112 cores; integrate gives 4.5x vs TBB and 14x vs OpenMP. Abstract averages: 2.7x faster and 6.2x less memory than TBB; 7.2x faster and 10x less memory than libomp.
corrections.workload: Fork-join benchmarks: recursive fib(42), numerical integration, matmul, nqueens(14), and UTS geometric (T1L, T1XXL) and binomial (T3L, T3XXL) trees. Execution time (Google Benchmark, median of 5 runs) and peak RSS (GNU time) are measured, swept over 1-112 cores.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Clang 18.0.0 (LLVM commit c4b795df) at the 'highest optimization setting' with runtime asserts disabled (exact flag string not listed). Uses libomp bundled with Clang, TBB 2021.10.0, taskflow 3.6.0 and libfork 3.5.0.
corrections.hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ (2.0 GHz, boost to 3.8 GHz), 112 cores across 2 NUMA nodes, 500 GiB RAM
corrections.caveats: arXiv preprint (v1, 28 Feb 2024) with no journal or conference reference listed. The 'up to' headline figures are peak ratios on the very fine-grained fib/integrate benchmarks at 112 cores. The averages in the abstract are lower: 2.7x vs TBB, 7.2x vs libomp. The paper describes flags only as 'highest optimization setting'. Independent corroboration with explicit -O3 -march=native comes from tzcnt/runtime-benchmarks, where libfork beats tbb 1.14x-3.9x. The baseline beaten is oneTBB/OpenMP/Taskflow, not std::async/std::thread/std::future.

notes: The record's 'up to' numbers are verbatim from the paper's conclusion (and the README). Hardware and compiler were in the PDF, which was the reason for the earlier Tier C cap, so the tier moves up to A. The default-branch (main) last commit is 2026-01-17; pushed_at 2026-05-25 reflects non-default branches (dev-v4, modules, etc.). It is still active.

tier_reason: The README benchmark table compares ThreadPool against std::async (std::launch::async) using the public benchmark/benchmark.cpp. It gives no CPU model or compiler, and CMakeLists.txt sets no build type or -O flags, so the documented build is unoptimized by default. First-party numbers with thin methodology: Tier C.

corrections.caveats: No CPU model, compiler or optimization flags are stated. CMakeLists.txt sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE and only -Wall -Wextra, so the documented `cmake -B build` produces an unoptimized build, likely -O0 (Tier C cap). Each variant is timed once at millisecond resolution, with no repetitions or warm-up; the single-threaded baseline runs first. The table shows implausible superlinear speedups on a 4-core machine (3.2x with 2 threads, 9.7x with 8 threads), which points to measurement artifacts. The std::async variant spawns 100 OS threads, so the win mostly measures thread-creation overhead. There is no LICENSE file (404) despite an MIT badge in the README, so usability is 'reference'. Zero stars; single-author project.

notes: The claimed numbers match the README table (10ms/7ms vs 18ms; 6.8x and 3.8x vs the 68ms single-threaded run) and the derived markers are present. The record is kept at Tier C, but the evidence is weak: likely unoptimized build, single run, superlinear speedups. Metadata matches: no license, 0 stars, last commit 2026-04-01, active.
